title: A stock, not a year's worth of households
text: The official temporary-accommodation count is a snapshot at the end of a quarter. It does not count every household that passed through accommodation during the year. In this scenario, pressure continues even when the accommodation allocation falls: less funding does not remove the need for a place to stay.
reason: Temporary-accommodation need remains after your decision.

title: An empty home is not always ready to let
text: Table 615 separates all-tenure vacant dwellings from homes owned by local authorities. These categories also have different snapshot dates. Neither measure identifies homes that can immediately be offered to households in temporary accommodation. The scenario's eligible pool is a separate, illustrative assumption, with a finite delivery capacity and a cost for works.
reason: Your delivery choices draw on a limited assumed pool.

title: The wait for repairs matters
text: Newham's published tenant survey reports that 65% of respondents who had received a repair were satisfied with the time taken in 2024–25. This is a measure of residents' experience, not a count of outstanding repair jobs. The model's repair backlog is illustrative and does not estimate illness or the experiences of individual residents.
reason: The repair allocation affects a separate modelled backlog.

title: Gross spending is not the council's net cost
text: The revenue-outturn return reports expenditure and income separately. House London adds the six direct temporary-accommodation categories and excludes administration. Its cash comparison uses gross accommodation expenditure throughout. It includes the full cost of new interventions, so an avoided accommodation cost is not automatically a net saving or cash that can be spent twice.
reason: Your total programme cost includes more than accommodation.
